units: the writer has settled not far from a harbour area
he lists the vehicles he has at his disposal
the small boat belongs to his neighbour
he has learnt to cast off the rope that holds the boat
his bicycle is old and needs seeing to every week
he uses it to reach the market
an animal pulls the cart
the craftsman strengthened the pulling gear
the shared boat leaves a trail on the water
the load he has to shift decides which one he takes
text: Dear friend, now that I have established myself a short distance from the harbour, let me describe how I travel about here. There are four means, and I use each of them in turn. The first is my neighbour's rowing boat, and I have finally learnt to cast off the mooring rope without fumbling. The second is a bicycle, ancient and remarkably heavy, which I overhaul every week before riding down to the covered market. The third is a cart drawn by a donkey, with a harness that the wheelwright strengthened before the cold weather arrived. The fourth is the river ferry, which leaves a broad, unhurried trail behind it. What settles the question, I must admit, is simply whatever happens to need carrying. With every good wish, and in the sincere hope of welcoming you here before long.

units: training opens with a spell of watching at the landing stage
the novice first learns to handle the steering
he then sails as second hand on working crossings
approach drills are done in still water to begin with
the difficulty rises when a headwind is added
the test includes a crossing made in darkness
a breakdown is staged on purpose during the trial
the final berthing is carried out with no engine
the newly qualified pilot works under an old hand for a season
shipping firms are wary of pilots with little experience
text: How does the training of a river ferry pilot begin? With a spell at the landing stage, where the learner watches the manoeuvres and gets the feel of the tiller without forcing it. What follows afterwards? The candidate sails as second hand on working crossings, repeating the approaches in still water at first, then against a headwind. What closes the course? A crossing made in darkness, a breakdown staged deliberately, and a final berthing with the engine shut down. Why does that last one matter? Because it makes the crew read the current and watch the wash of passing craft. Is the certificate enough to take charge? Certainly not. The newly qualified pilot must still work under an old hand for a whole season. Shipping firms welcome such caution, and rarely hand a deck over to a beginner.

units: the courier takes off his head gear before speaking
a slippery layer covered the road surface
his two-wheeler lost its grip on a bend
the driving wheel span without biting into the ground
he insists that he did not come off
he weaved between heavy lorries to keep out of the ditch
a parcel dropped from the rack at the back
he turned back to pick the parcel up
his round ran late
he took a picture of the wheel to convince his supervisor
text: The courier set his helmet down on the table and started explaining. He said the roadway had been covered in a fine slick of mud, and that his scooter had slithered sideways on the lower bend. The back wheel, he said, span uselessly without biting the moment he opened the throttle rather too hard. I asked whether he had come off, because he was limping slightly as he came indoors. He said he had not, but that he had weaved between two heavy lorries to keep himself out of the ditch. The parcel had worked loose from the rack behind and dropped, so he doubled back to retrieve it, and his delivery round ended up running late. His supervisor, he told me, never believes stories involving mud. So he had photographed the filthy wheel before setting off again, simply to have something convincing to show.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: changing track once called for heavy work done by hand
workers had to lever the rolling stock up and shove it across
the growing number of lines made the problem sharper
a man in a repair shed thought up a device with swinging blades
one pull on a lever was enough to move those blades
from then on the train changed direction while still rolling
the system had few parts and was easy to mend
this invention helped the lines grow into a network
students of the history of engineering see a decisive step in it
text: Sending a rail waggon down another track once meant taking the whole thing apart: men levered the wheels clear with bars, then shoved the frame across by main strength. Every junction cost a morning of exhausting labour. The operators wanted a way out, for the lines were multiplying and crossings came thick and fast. A fitter in a repair shed suggested hinging two movable steel blades against the fixed rails, so that one pull on a lever would swing them aside. From then on a train changed direction while still rolling. The idea spread quickly, since it took few parts and could be mended on the spot. It also reshaped the way track was laid: builders stopped stringing out lonely lines and began weaving webs where every branch met the next. Historians of engineering call it a founding step.

units: the two ways of getting about look alike but spend energy differently
the walker has to lift his own weight at every stride
his energy drains away into a movement he repeats
the cyclist lets the saddle carry his weight
he keeps up a turning motion that the wheel holds on to
for the same effort the bicycle covers a greater distance
walking needs no machinery at all
it gets over obstacles that a wheel cannot take
the machine offers speed but stays fragile
the kind of ground should guide the traveller in choosing
text: Walking and cycling look like near neighbours, yet the way each spends energy differs sharply. The walker lifts his own weight at every stride, sets it down, then lifts it again; his effort drains away into a stubborn, repeated beat. The cyclist hands that weight over to a saddle and has only to keep a turning motion alive, which the wheel then carries on for him. Hence a striking difference: for the same effort, the bicycle takes its rider considerably further than his legs alone would manage. Walking, though, holds a quieter advantage. It asks for no chain, no inner tube, no smooth roadway, and it climbs the stair, crosses the bramble, survives the soft sand. One buys speed and pays with a fragile machine, the other buys freedom and pays in slowness. A wise traveller reads the ground before deciding.

units: the customer reports a sway that shows up at speed
the check is worked through one station at a time
the coupling part had too much play in it
that play set the load lurching on a cambered surface
the tyres showed slanting wear on the inner side
such wear gives away a fault in the tracking of the wheels
one clamp on the suspension had lost its grip
the braking system worked but was clogged up
the road test after the repair showed no sway at all
the driver had been running in that state for weeks
text: A driver left his trailer with us one wet evening, reporting a persistent sway that appeared as soon as the pace picked up. We worked through it station by station. First station: the coupling ball, where the play ran well beyond what is permitted, enough on its own to set the whole rig lurching on a cambered surface. Second station: the tyres, worn on a slant along the inner shoulder, the unmistakable sign of tracking gone out. Third station: the leaf suspension, one clamp of which had lost its grip entirely. Fourth station: the braking circuit, sound but thoroughly clogged with grime. We fitted a fresh ball, reset the axle, pulled the clamps up again and bled the lines. On the road test the sway had disappeared, and the driver owned up to having run like that for weeks on end.

units: the first check is on how hard the tyres are blown up
a soft tyre slides on wet ground
the drive is to be looked over next
the braking faces must be free of any damp
the saddle is set so that the leg is nearly straight at the bottom of the stroke
the bags are shared out on either side of the back wheel
an uneven load makes the ride unsteady on a slope
something is carried to mend a puncture
a brake test comes before joining the traffic
text: Before you set off, please work through the following operations in the order given. Begin with the tyres, squeezing each one firmly between thumb and forefinger, since soft rubber slides about on a wet roadway. Move on to the chain and its tension, then to the brake blocks, whose faces must remain perfectly clean and thoroughly dry. Adjust the saddle so that the leg comes almost straight at the bottom of the pedal stroke. Hang the panniers either side of the back wheel, matching the loads carefully on each flank; get that wrong and the machine will wander alarmingly on the very first descent. Pack a spare inner tube, a pair of tyre levers and a pump. Finish with a short run along a level path, squeezing the brakes on gradually, and only afterwards venture into the traffic.

units: a crossing structure has been shut for renovation
vehicles now take a narrow road along the heights
lorries have trouble passing one another there
the daily run to work now takes twice as long
the buses that carry people about are running late
the shops in the lower quarter are losing custom
the local authority has put link boats into service
this measure does not settle the question of goods
the metal frame had been eaten away by rust
the work should be finished before the cold season ends
text: Shutting the bridge for renovation has thrown the whole town's traffic out of shape. Vehicles now climb a narrow ridge road where lorries can barely squeeze past one another. The consequence appeared immediately: the daily run to work takes twice as long, and the works buses arrive noticeably late. Traders in the lower streets report a clear drop in custom, since shoppers give up on the detour. The council has answered by hiring two river shuttles, which link the banks at frequent intervals. The stopgap absorbs a share of those travelling on foot, yet it leaves deliveries exactly where they were. An engineer on site explains that the metal frame had been eaten away by rust, and that patching it would never have held. The work is due to finish before the cold season is out.

units: the way up is made of gravel and looks to be in poor repair
it climbs steeply and forks at the top
the hollows in the ground shake vehicles about badly
rain turns the surface slippery
the wheels lose their grip on the run into the bend
someone living nearby decided to do something about it
he brought crushed stone up to fill the holes
he cut a drain along the bank
the ground now dries out quickly
dust lifts when towed vehicles go by
text: Our gravel track has never been particularly handsome, and there is no point whatever in pretending otherwise. It climbs steeply, it turns sharply at the fork near the summit, and the ruts run so deep that a car rocks about like an old rowing boat. In rain the surface turns soapy and the wheels slither on the approach to the bend; you grip the steering wheel with both hands and hope that nothing is descending towards you. The neighbour below eventually had enough of it. He brought up a load of crushed stone, filled the hollows, then cut a channel along the embankment to carry the water away. The slope dries out quickly now and the mud no longer accumulates. Perfect it certainly is not, since dust lifts whenever a trailer passes, but one can finally drive up without apprehension.

units: the piece sets widening the roads against building up the railway
a queue of cars takes up a wide strip of ground for very few people
a train on rails carries as many people on less space
those who stand up for the car point to its being there at any hour
that advantage counts above all where few people live
towns that have widened their main roads see the jams come back
that return of saturation happens very quickly
a service running to a steady timetable takes on the growth in numbers
the writer argues for putting money first into the lasting answer
text: Should we widen the fast roads once more, or pay for extra carriages on the railway? The question deserves a cool head. A queue of private cars occupies a great width of ground to shift a mere handful of people, whereas a train on rails carries the same crowd on a far narrower strip. Those who stand up for the car object that it goes anywhere, at any hour, with no changes and no waiting; the point holds, above all away from crowded districts. Yet towns that have doubled their main roads watch the flow fill those additional lanes within a single season. A line running to a steady timetable, by contrast, absorbs the growth without choking. Our own position is perfectly plain: widening relieves briefly, timetabling relieves lastingly. Public money should go first to what does not silt up again.
